Dog runs built for Montverde's sloped lots

Pet turf in Montverde runs $10–$18 a square foot installed, typically $12–$16, as of September 2026. A dog run on a ridge-top lot has the opposite drainage problem most Florida yards have: the ground here lets go of water so fast that keeping infill in place, not moving it out, is the real design question.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a 300 sq ft run on a graded slope

Say you have a 300 sq ft dog run planned down a side yard that drops nearly three feet from top to bottom, typical of a ridge lot away from the two lakes. At the typical pet-turf rate of $12 to $16 a square foot, that runs about $3,600 to $4,800, with the coarser infill grain and reinforced downhill edge included in that figure rather than billed as an add-on. A flat run of the same size near Oakland or Winter Garden would use the same range without the extra anchoring step.

Excessively drained sand means the run never puddles

Astatula and Candler sand pass water fast enough that a dog run built on either one is unlikely to hold standing urine or rainwater the way a run on Osceola County's flatwoods sand might. That's good news for odor control, but it means zeolite or a coated infill still earns its keep for ammonia release rather than drainage, since the sand underneath was never the bottleneck to begin with.

What the manufacturer's spec sheet adds for a wet-use backing

A fully permeable backing built for a Montverde dog run still comes with its own manufacturer spec for seam adhesive and infill rate, and following it matters more here than on a plain lawn since that backing sees far more standing moisture from daily rinsing than an ordinary residential product does. An adhesive rated for occasional dampness on a lawn install can fail faster under a pet system's near-daily wet cycle, which is why a pet-rated product's spec sheet often calls for a different bonding agent even though the visible seaming step looks identical. Following the specific product's documentation, not a general lawn install habit, is what the installed-to-specification standard actually asks for here.

A sloped run needs a harder edge than a flat one

A dog run angled down a Montverde ridge lot loses infill to gravity faster than one on level ground, especially once a dog's regular running path packs the surface and gives loose material an easier route downhill. We anchor the downhill perimeter more heavily on these runs and pick a coarser grain of infill, since Florida's rule requires infill to stay on the property and a fine sand migrates first on a real grade.

Why a dog run's drain point can't aim at the street

A Montverde corner lot often carries a drainage swale along both street frontages, and the state's rule against installing turf inside a swale rules out sending a dog run's higher liquid volume toward either one, unlike a plain lawn that sometimes has more flexibility in where its grade exits. Instead, a run on a corner lot gets graded inward, toward a point still on the property, even if that means a slightly longer routed slope than a straight shot to the nearest street-side ditch would offer. Losing the easy option doesn't change the one to two percent grade itself, only which direction it has to travel to reach a legal drain point.

When odor infill leaves the yard during a storm

The state's rule against infill washing off the property applies to a Montverde dog run's zeolite or coated sand as much as it does to any lawn's silica, and a run graded too steeply toward its drain point can carry a visible amount of infill past the property line during a hard rain, sometimes into a neighbor's yard downhill. That's a different failure than the run simply smelling because of a shallow base; it's a drainage and grading problem showing up as material loss rather than odor. A gentler grade at the drain point and a properly finished edge there keep infill from becoming the storm's collateral damage.

The hose test a dog run gets before its first use

Once a Montverde dog run's last step of infill is brushed in, running a hose across the full footprint and watching where water goes is worth doing before a dog is ever let onto it, confirming the drain point actually clears standing water within roughly a minute the way the deeper base and permeable backing are built to. This test also surfaces any lingering odor from construction dust or adhesive before the run gets its first real use. Catching a slow spot on this walkthrough, while the crew is still on site, is simpler than tracing a smell back to a drainage issue weeks later.

What to note about a run on handoff day

Right when a Montverde dog run's crew finishes, noting exactly where the gate threshold sits and confirming the drain point clears a hose test quickly pays off later, since both are easier to point to on day one than to relocate from memory months after the surrounding lawn has grown in around them. This is also the moment to ask which infill went in, zeolite or coated sand, since future top-ups work best matching the original product rather than mixing two different odor-control materials in the same run. A few minutes of notes on handoff day saves guesswork the first time something needs checking.

Staying clear of Lake Apopka's edge on a shoreline lot

A handful of Montverde lots run down to Lake Apopka itself, and a dog run planned near that edge still needs the state's 10-ft waterbody setback measured in before layout, seawall lots excepted. Combined with a slope, that setback can eat more of the usable yard than a homeowner expects, which is worth confirming before ordering material rather than after.

Questions people ask

Does a sloped yard change which infill works best for dogs?

It changes the grain size more than the material. Zeolite and coated sand both still work for odor control; we lean toward a coarser grade of whichever one you choose so it resists sliding downhill.

Can a dog run in Montverde go right up to Lake Apopka's shoreline?

Not without a seawall or bulkhead already in place. Otherwise the state's 10-ft setback from the water's edge applies the same as it would on any other Central Florida lake lot.
